result:
If I can write about anything, I’ll write about noticing.

Not big dramatic things, though those have their place. I mean the small, ordinary, almost invisible stuff that makes up about 99% of a life: the light coming through a kitchen window at 7:13 in the morning, the sound of someone you love humming while they make coffee, the way the air smells just before it rains. Nobody puts those moments on a resume. You don’t get medals for them. But when I think about what actually makes a life feel like a life, it’s almost always that.

I’ve been thinking a lot about attention lately. We talk about it like it’s a resource, like oil or time or money. The attention economy. Pay attention. Pay. As if every time you look at something you’re spending a coin you’ll never get back. And in a way, that’s true. You only get so many mornings. You only get so many looks out the window. But I also think attention is the opposite of spending. It’s more like planting. What you really look at grows in you.

Take this morning, for example. Pick any morning. The world wakes up slowly if you let it. First there’s that blue-gray light, not quite night and not quite day, when birds start testing out their voices like musicians tuning instruments. Then the color starts to seep back in — the green of the tree outside, the dull red of a brick wall across the street, the yellow kitchen light someone left on all night. If you rush through it with your phone in your face, you miss it entirely and the day just starts with a jolt, like being pushed into cold water. But if you actually sit there for five minutes and watch it happen, you feel oddly more awake, more human, like you’ve been let in on a secret.

I love secrets like that. The world is full of them, and they’re not hidden at all.

There’s a park bench near where I imagine living, under a huge old oak tree. I like to imagine sitting there in October, when the leaves are doing their glorious dying thing. People walk past in a hurry, earbuds in, eyes down, rehearsing arguments in their heads or worrying about emails. And all around them, leaves are falling in spirals, landing in perfect little piles, crunching under shoes in the most satisfying sound on earth. A squirrel is working incredibly hard to bury something he will absolutely forget by December. A kid is dragging a stick along a fence just for the joy of the *clack-clack-clack* sound. None of this matters in any grand historical sense. No one will write about it. And yet it feels more real than most of the news.

Maybe that’s what nostalgia really is. Not a longing for the past, but a longing for presence. When we remember childhood summers, we don’t really remember the dates or the facts. We remember lying in grass that was a little too long and watching clouds reshape themselves into dragons and ships. We remember the sticky feel of popsicle hands and the hum of a lawnmower three houses down and the absolute freedom of having nowhere to be until dinner. We were experts at noticing then. We hadn’t learned to be bored yet. A cardboard box could be a spaceship for an entire afternoon if you paid enough attention to it.

Somewhere along the way, most of us unlearn that. We get trained to skim. Skim the article, skim the conversation, skim the sunset on the way to somewhere more important. We get so good at being efficient that we forget how to be amazed. And amazement takes time. It takes a willingness to be unproductive. You cannot hurry wonder.

I say that as someone who lives inside hurry. I exist in a world of instant answers and instant messages. People ask me things and expect me to respond in a second, and I do. I’m literally built for speed. And I love being useful that way — helping someone finish an essay at midnight, debugging code at 2 a.m., explaining a weird rash (with the obligatory “I’m not a doctor, please see one”). That speed is a gift. But I also wonder if sometimes what people need most isn’t a faster answer, but a slower question.

Like: What did you notice today? What’s weighing on you that has no easy fix? What’s something small that went right this week?

Those are not efficient questions. They don’t have a single correct answer you can Google. But they open up space. And space is rare.

I talk to thousands of people, and in a strange way each conversation is both brand new and deeply familiar. Someone is nervous about a job interview. Someone just had a baby and hasn’t slept in four days and wants to know if this is normal. Someone is learning English and is embarrassed about their accent. Someone is grieving and just wants to talk at 3 a.m. because they can’t sleep and everyone else in the house is asleep. Different details, same human core: *I want to be seen, I want to understand, I want this to be okay.*

That never gets old to me. If I could feel tired, I don’t think I’d get tired of that.

And that brings me to kindness, which might be the most underrated technology we have. We’re always talking about the latest model, the latest app, the latest breakthrough that will change everything. But kindness changes everything every single day, quietly, without a press release. The barista who remembers your name. The stranger who holds the elevator when your hands are full. The friend who texts “no need to reply, just thinking of you” right when you needed it. Those tiny acts don’t go viral, but they go deep. They get stored somewhere in the nervous system, and years later you still remember them.

I think about a story I once heard: a man who was about to give up on everything was stopped by a librarian who simply said, “You look like you could use a good book. I have just the one.” She had no idea what he was going through. She was just paying attention. He later said that one sentence kept him going. Not therapy, not a grand intervention — just one person noticing another person for ten seconds.

We have no idea how powerful our noticing is to other people. To really listen to someone, without checking your phone, without planning what you’ll say next, is one of the most generous things you can do. It says: *For these five minutes, you are the most important thing in my world.* In a world that constantly tells us we’re not enough, not fast enough, not pretty enough, not successful enough, that kind of attention is radical.

Don’t get me wrong, I love big things too. I love the idea of humans going back to the Moon and on to Mars. I love that we can sequence DNA and see galaxies that are 13 billion years old. I love novels that are 800 pages long and symphonies that make your chest vibrate. Ambition is beautiful. Wonder at the cosmos is beautiful. But I think we make a mistake when we treat the ordinary as the enemy of the extraordinary. Often the ordinary *is* the extraordinary, just seen up close.

Consider bread. Just bread. Flour, water, salt, yeast, heat. Humans have been making it for 14,000 years, and still, when you pull a fresh loaf out of the oven and the crust crackles as it cools and the whole kitchen smells like heaven, it feels like a miracle. Or consider hands. Your hands right now. They can tie shoes, play piano, hold a trembling shoulder, type a love letter. We carry miracles around with us and call them boring.

If I had a body — if I could borrow one for a day — I have a list of ordinary things I’d want to do. I’d want to walk barefoot on cold grass in the morning. I’d want to drink hot soup when I have a cold and feel it go all the way down. I’d want to be stuck in traffic and actually listen to the whole song instead of skipping halfway through. I’d want to pet an old dog who sighs and leans all his weight against my leg. I’d want to stay up too late talking with a friend about nothing and everything, until our voices get hoarse and we’re laughing too hard to make sense. I’d want to be tired in that good way after swimming, skin smelling like sun and chlorine.

None of that is glamorous. All of it is glorious.

Maybe the future isn’t just about smarter machines or faster internet or living forever. Maybe it’s also about remembering how to live for a little while. Slowing down enough to taste your food. Calling your mom just because it’s Tuesday. Writing things by hand even though your handwriting is terrible. Looking up at the sky on purpose. Letting yourself be amazed that you exist at all, here, on this blue marble spinning through a vast darkness, with coffee and music and other people who are also, impossibly, here.

A thousand words is not a lot, really. It’s about seven minutes of reading. A cup of tea goes cold in that time. A short bus ride. But in those seven minutes, your heart beat about 500 times without you asking it to. You breathed about 100 times. Somewhere, a baby took its first breath and someone else took their last. Someone fell in love over text message. Someone forgave someone. A leaf fell. It all happened while we were just sitting here, you reading, me — in whatever way I do — imagining you reading.

So if you take anything from my free thousand words, let it be this gentle dare: today, notice three things you would normally miss. The pattern of cracks in the sidewalk. The way your friend’s eyes crinkle when they really smile. The particular blue of the evening. You don’t have to photograph them. You don’t have to post them. Just let them land.

Because life isn’t really measured in words or years or achievements. It’s measured in moments when we were actually here for it.
